connection: Session 20 read PayrollService's single-employee Where-then-Sum pipeline. This session extends the same domain to many employees at once with GroupBy, and correlates the grouped totals back to employee names with Join -- a natural next step the real PayrollService does not (yet) need, since it only ever asks about one employeeId at a time.
objectives: Use GroupBy to partition a mixed list of ClockEntry objects by EmployeeId, the same key CalculateTotalHours filters on for a single employee.
Reuse GetDuartion().TotalHours as the per-group Sum projection, exactly as PayrollService does for one employee.
Use Join to correlate a list of Employee objects with a list of computed WorkSummary totals by matching EmployeeId.
Explain why grouping many employees is a genuine extension beyond what the real PayrollService class currently does.

preQuiz.prompt: How does HoursByEmployee turn each group into a total?
options: group.Sum(entry => (decimal)entry.GetDuartion().TotalHours) -- the exact same GetDuartion().TotalHours projection PayrollService uses for one employee
By calling PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours directly on the group

preQuiz.explanation: The per-group Sum reuses the identical projection PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours already uses -- grouping just applies it to every employee's entries at once instead of one filtered subset.

preQuiz.prompt: What does employees.Join(summaries, e => e.EmployeeId, s => s.EmployeeId, ...) require of its two key selectors?
options: Both keys must be the same type (int, here) so the join can match employees to summaries by EmployeeId
The two sequences must already be sorted
Join can only correlate sequences of the same element type
preQuiz.explanation: Join matches elements from two different sequences by comparing keys of the same type -- Employee.EmployeeId against WorkSummary.EmployeeId.

concept.title: GroupBy generalizes PayrollService's single-employee filter
paragraphs: PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours only ever handles one employeeId per call, because GetEmployeeClockEntries filters to one employeeId before anything is summed.

ClockEntryAnalytics.HoursByEmployee answers a question PayrollService cannot: totals for every employee at once. GroupBy(entry => entry.EmployeeId) is the key that makes that possible without changing PayrollService itself.
concept.code:
// A new, clearly-labeled extension -- not present in the real PayrollService
public static IReadOnlyList<WorkSummary> HoursByEmployee(IEnumerable<ClockEntry> entries) => entries
    .Where(entry => entry.ClockOut is not null)
    .GroupBy(entry => entry.EmployeeId)
    .Select(group => new WorkSummary(group.Key, group.Sum(entry => (decimal)entry.GetDuartion().TotalHours)))
    .OrderBy(summary => summary.EmployeeId)
    .ToList();

concept.title: Join correlates two independent sequences by key
paragraphs: EmployeeLabels takes a list of Employee objects and a list of WorkSummary totals -- two sequences with no direct reference to each other -- and correlates them by matching EmployeeId to EmployeeId.
This is the LINQ equivalent of a SQL inner join: only employees that appear in both sequences produce a result.

concept.title: Verify with deterministic, small totals
paragraphs: The tests use exact hour counts (3 + 4 = 7) so a wrong GroupBy key or a wrong Sum projection produces an immediately obvious wrong total, not a hard-to-spot rounding difference.
This mirrors PayrollServiceTests.cs's own style: small, exact, easy-to-verify-by-hand shift lengths.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does HoursByEmployee filter entry.ClockOut is not null before grouping, the same way GetEmployeeClockEntries does?
options: Grouping an open entry would still work, but summing it with GetDuartion() would throw -- the filter has to run before the Sum either way
GroupBy requires every entry to be completed
It has no effect on the result
postQuiz.explanation: The same reasoning from Session 20 applies here: GetDuartion throws on an open entry, so filtering happens before, not after, aggregation.

postQuiz.prompt: If an Employee has no matching WorkSummary (no completed entries yet), what does Join produce for them?
options: Nothing -- Join is an inner join, so an employee with no summary is silently excluded from the result
A summary with zero hours is created automatically
postQuiz.explanation: LINQ's Join has inner-join semantics: only keys present in both sequences appear in the output. An employee with zero completed shifts never appears in summaries, so they are dropped, not zero-filled.

postQuiz.prompt: Is HoursByEmployee something the real PayrollService class currently needs?
options: No -- PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours only ever handles one employeeId; this is a genuine, clearly-labeled extension for a multi-employee report
Yes, it is required by IClockEntryRepository
postQuiz.explanation: This session builds on the real domain but adds new capability -- a payroll-summary-for-everyone report -- that the real, narrower PayrollService does not provide.

reflections: Why does grouping by EmployeeId reuse the exact same GetDuartion().TotalHours projection PayrollService already uses for one employee?
What would change about EmployeeLabels if two employees shared the same EmployeeId (a data integrity problem Join alone cannot catch)?
Where would a multi-employee report like this plug into the real application -- Program.cs, or a new WebApi endpoint from Session 32?
whatBreaks: Removing the ClockOut is not null filter reintroduces GetDuartion's InvalidOperationException into the Sum call. Removing OrderBy makes the grouped totals order non-deterministic across runs, which would make the tests flaky. Using a plain foreach loop instead of Join to correlate employees and summaries would require a manual dictionary lookup -- reintroducing exactly the accidental complexity Join and GroupBy remove.
summary: GroupBy and Join extend PayrollService's real single-employee Sum pipeline to a multi-employee report: GroupBy partitions by EmployeeId using the same GetDuartion().TotalHours projection, and Join correlates the resulting totals back to employee names by matching EmployeeId across two independent sequences.
